screens.title: Connecting to the Blockchain: Web3.js and Ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on the practical plumbing that lets a browser-based DApp speak to Ethereum. You will learn why libraries like web3. js and ethers. js exist, how they wrap the node JSON‑RPC A P I, and what a provider and a signer do for your application. We'll show concrete provider types you will use in the browser or from services like Infura and Alchemy, and we'll walk through a typical wallet connection flow so your frontend can read the network and ask the user to sign transactions. This matters because a correct provider and a secure signer are the difference between read-only data calls and safely sending state-changing transactions. For example, using a BrowserProvider lets MetaMask hold private keys while your app requests a signed transaction. A common trap is treating a JsonRpcProvider as if it could sign; it cannot. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to initialize ethers. js providers, request account access, fetch the current block number, and respond to account or chain changes with safe patterns. Think about your own DApp: what operations will require a signer, and which can use a read-only provider?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Connecting to the Blockchain

Connecting to the Blockchain

Use web3.js or ethers.js to wrap node RPC, choose the right provider, and request a signer for transactions.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson
Why providers, signers, and wallet connections matter.
Coming up
BrowserProvider, JsonRpcProvider, and example connect code.
Hands-on
Add ConnectWallet.jsx to your React app and test with MetaMask.
Concept map
Provider
Connects to node (BrowserProvider, JsonRpcProvider)
Signer
Signs transactions via wallet (MetaMask)
Quick example
const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
await provider.send('eth_requestAccounts', []);
const signer = await provider.getSigner();
Key Takeaway

Choose the correct provider for your needs: use BrowserProvider for signed transactions in the browser and JsonRpcProvider for read-only access from services.

Live Coding Brief

We will install ethers, create ConnectWallet.jsx, and wire it into App.jsx. The code demonstrates BrowserProvider, requesting accounts, and reading the block number.

Why it matters

Correctly connecting protects private keys, ensures accurate network data, and enables seamless user prompts for signing transactions.

Explore Key Topics
Providers: Browser vs JsonRpc. Signers and transaction signing. Common mistakes such as assuming JsonRpcProvider signs.

screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to name and use the main libraries that connect a DApp to Ethereum, initialize providers, and request a signer for transactions. First, you'll distinguish the roles of web3. js and ethers. js and why ethers. js is often chosen for frontend work. Second, you'll configure BrowserProvider for injected wallets and JsonRpcProvider for read‑only access, which is important when your app must fetch data without holding private keys. Third, you'll retrieve basic blockchain data such as the current block number and network ID so your UI can display accurate state. Finally, you'll recognize common connection pitfalls like missing window. ethereum or assuming a provider can sign. Each objective is practical and directly maps to tasks you will run in your project, ensuring your DApp can both read data and securely request signed transactions from users. screens.title: What web3.js and ethers.js do
screens.narratorSegment: At the heart of a DApp's communication layer are libraries that hide the raw JSON‑RPC details and present a higher‑level A P I. web3. js and ethers. js both serve this role, but the chapter emphasizes that ethers. js was designed for a cleaner, modular developer experience. Conceptually both libraries translate method calls into JSON‑RPC requests that a node understands. For example, a call to get the current block number becomes a JSON‑RPC call the library abstracts away. A concrete example is calling provider. getBlockNumber in ethers. js: the library performs the RPC, returns a number, and allows your UI to display the latest block. A common misconception is that libraries add new network capabilities; they only wrap the node A P I and provide utilities like ABI encoding, contract binding, and convenience helpers. Another common confusion is believing one library is more secure simply by name; security comes from correct usage, provider choice, and not exposing private keys. Closing thought: when choosing a library, prioritize the A P I ergonomics and the patterns that match your stack, especially if you use TypeScript and want stronger type guarantees.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: web3.js and ethers.js are client libraries that wrap JSON‑RPC to simplify blockchain interaction from the frontend.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What web3.js and ethers.js do
Definition

These libraries act as wrappers for the node JSON‑RPC API, converting developer calls into RPC requests and returning parsed responses.

Concrete example
Calling provider.getBlockNumber returns the latest block index, freeing you from manual RPC request handling.
Common misconception
These libraries do not change network capabilities; they provide ergonomics, encoding helpers, and contract bindings.
Why it matters
Using a well‑designed library reduces bugs and helps you focus on app logic rather than low-level RPC calls.
Analogy

Think of the library as a driver: the browser app speaks a friendly language and the library translates it into the node's RPC dialect.

Quick call examples
// ethers.js style
const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider('https://...');
const block = await provider.getBlockNumber();
Key Takeaway

Pick the library that matches your ergonomics and type needs; both wrap the node API and provide contract helpers.

screens.title: web3.js vs ethers.js
screens.narratorSegment: Both libraries provide the same core capability: talk to Ethereum nodes. The chapter emphasizes their design differences. web3. js is older and very comprehensive; it bundles many modules and covers many interaction needs. ethers. js was built later with modularity, smaller bundles, and a focus on security and developer ergonomics, including TypeScript friendliness. A concrete example: when building a Vite React frontend, many developers prefer ethers. js because it is lighter to bundle and its BrowserProvider integrates nicely with an injected wallet. A common mistake is choosing a library solely on age or popularity; instead evaluate A P I ergonomics, size, and TypeScript support that match your stack. Also, realize that switching between them does not change node behavior since both ultimately call JSON‑RPC. Closing question: which matters more for your project — a feature-heavy A P I or smaller client size and clearer TypeScript types? That choice should guide your selection. web3.js vs ethers.js means web3.js is comprehensive and older; ethers.js is modular, lightweight, and often preferred for frontend typescript work.. In practical terms, design philosophy, modularity, and frontend preferences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › web3.js vs ethers.js
web3.js

An older, feature-rich library created early in the Ethereum ecosystem with broad API coverage.

Strength
Comprehensive API surface for many node interactions.
Consideration
Larger bundle and older patterns may not align with modern TypeScript usage.
ethers.js

Modern, modular, and often preferred for frontend DApp development for its smaller footprint and TypeScript friendliness.

Strength
Cleaner API, better modularization, and improved developer experience.
Consideration
Some very specialized utilities may be more mature in web3.js depending on use case.
Decision tip

If you prioritize bundle size, clarity, and TypeScript support in the browser, ethers.js is often the better fit. If you need exhaustive legacy functionality, web3.js remains usable.

screens.title: What is a Provider?
screens.narratorSegment: A provider is the object that allows a library like ethers. js to speak to an Ethereum node. It is responsible for making JSON‑RPC requests on behalf of your application. There are several provider types you will use in practice. A BrowserProvider wraps an injected window. ethereum object offered by wallet extensions such as MetaMask and enables the wallet to manage keys and sign transactions. A JsonRpcProvider connects to a specific endpoint like an Infura or Alchemy URL and is ideal for read‑only access when you don't need to sign transactions. The chapter also mentions specialized constructors that simplify connecting to popular services. A concrete example: using JsonRpcProvider with an Infura endpoint to fetch historical blocks for display in a dashboard. A frequent misconception is thinking a provider can always sign—only providers that expose a signer or when combined with a Signer can sign. In short, choosing the right provider determines whether your app can only read blockchain data or also initiate signed transactions through a wallet. What is a Provider? means providers are the communication layer to nodes; browserprovider for injected wallets, jsonrpcprovider for read-only endpoints.. In practical terms, the abstraction that connects a library to an ethereum node. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What is a Provider?
Provider types
  • BrowserProvider: Wraps window.ethereum from wallets like MetaMask and enables signing via the wallet.
  • JsonRpcProvider: Connects to a node endpoint for read-only operations, such as Infura or a local Hardhat node.
  • Specialized providers: Convenience constructors for providers targeting popular services.
Concrete scenario

Use JsonRpcProvider when you want to fetch many blocks or logs from a reliable endpoint without asking the user to sign.

Misconception
A provider alone may not sign transactions. You need a Signer from a BrowserProvider or an explicit Wallet signer for signing.
Why this matters

Selecting the correct provider determines whether your DApp can initiate transactions, rely on user wallets for signing, or only read blockchain state reliably from a node service.

screens.title: BrowserProvider and injected wallets
screens.narratorSegment: Working with an injected wallet begins by detecting the injected provider object in the browser. The usual pattern is to check for window. ethereum and, if present, wrap it with ethers. BrowserProvider. That wrapper allows your app to request accounts and obtain a signer that delegates signing to the user's wallet. A concrete example from the chapter uses provider. send with the eth_requestAccounts method to prompt the user to connect. After accounts are granted, provider. getSigner returns the signer used to sign transactions. It is important to handle both outcomes: the user may deny permission or have no wallet installed. In such cases show a clear message and avoid throwing exceptions. Another key operational detail is listening to accountsChanged and chainChanged events on window. ethereum to update your app state when the user switches accounts or networks. A frequent mistake is failing to clear the signer when accounts are removed; handle an empty accounts array by resetting signer and account state. Finally, if chainChanged occurs, reinitialize or reload to ensure your provider matches the new network. keyIdea.text: Check window.ethereum, request accounts, get a signer, and listen for account or chain changes to keep the app state consistent.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › BrowserProvider and injected wallets
Step-by-step
  1. Check for window.ethereum. If absent, prompt user to install a wallet.
  2. Wrap with new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum).
  3. Call provider.send('eth_requestAccounts', []) to request permission.
  4. Obtain signer via provider.getSigner() for signing transactions.
  5. Listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged to update your UI.
Concrete code pattern
if (window.ethereum) {
  const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
  await provider.send('eth_requestAccounts', []);
  const signer = await provider.getSigner();
} else {
  // prompt to install a wallet
}
Mistake to avoid
Do not assume provider existence; always check window.ethereum and handle user denials gracefully.
Key Takeaway

BrowserProvider ties your DApp to the user's wallet for signing while keeping private keys out of your frontend code.

screens.title: JsonRpcProvider and specialized providers
screens.narratorSegment: A JsonRpcProvider connects directly to a JSON‑RPC endpoint and is typically used for non-signing tasks — reading blocks, fetching logs, or querying contract state. The chapter highlights that specialized constructors such as AlchemyProvider or InfuraProvider are convenience wrappers around JsonRpcProvider that simplify configuration for those services. A concrete scenario: if you run a block explorer or a dashboard that needs lots of historical data, JsonRpcProvider or an InfuraProvider gives you efficient, reliable access without needing user signatures. Remember that JsonRpcProvider cannot sign transactions on behalf of users in the browser: signing requires a signer obtained from an injected wallet or a server-side wallet with a private key. A common pitfall is to attempt to send a transaction through a JsonRpcProvider without a signer; that will fail because the provider has no private key to sign. Choose this provider for scalability and predictable read access, and pair it with BrowserProvider or a signer when you need to write to the chain. In practical terms, read-only access to nodes via endpoints like infura and alchemy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › JsonRpcProvider and specialized providers
When to use JsonRpcProvider

Choose this provider for dashboards, analytics, and any read-only work that needs a reliable node endpoint.

Specialized constructors

AlchemyProvider and InfuraProvider wrap JsonRpcProvider to reduce configuration friction with those services.

Practical note

If you need to submit transactions from the backend, use a Wallet signer with a private key on a secure server. Never place private keys in frontend code.

Core code (read-only display)
// ConnectWallet.jsx (excerpt)
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import { ethers } from 'ethers';

useEffect(() => {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    const ethProvider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
    setProvider(ethProvider);
  } else {
    setError('MetaMask not detected');
  }
}, []);

// connect flow
await provider.send('eth_requestAccounts', []);
const signer = await provider.getSigner();
const network = await provider.getNetwork();
const blockNumber = await provider.getBlockNumber();
Tip
Keep private keys out of the frontend. Use the signer handed by the wallet extension for secure signing.
Example output
Connected Account: 0x0123...abcd
Network: goerli
Current Block: 1234567

The ConnectWallet pattern gives you both read access and a signer for transactions after user consent.

What a Signer does

Signs messages and transactions using the account's private key. In browser flows, wallets do this for you securely.

Concrete example
Calling contract.connect(signer).functionName(...) sends a signed transaction that modifies chain state.
Misconception
A Provider alone cannot sign transactions unless combined with a Signer object that has access to private keys.
Security note

Never ask users for their private key in the frontend. Use the wallet to sign and keep private keys secured by the extension or hardware wallet.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Listening for account and chain changes
accountsChanged handling

When accounts change, update current account state and clear signer if no accounts remain to avoid sending unsigned requests.

Code pattern
window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', (newAccounts) => {
  setAccount(newAccounts[0] || null);
  if (!newAccounts.length) setSigner(null);
});
chainChanged handling

On chain change, reload or reinitialize to ensure network-specific settings and contract addresses are accurate.

Practical tip
A full reload is the simplest safe option for basic apps; for advanced apps, reinitialize provider and re-fetch network state.
Mistake to avoid

Failing to remove listeners on unmount can create duplicated handlers and unexpected behavior when components remount during navigation.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter lists several common mistakes that often cause broken DApp experiences. First, failing to check for window. ethereum leads to runtime errors; always detect the injected provider and provide a helpful message if absent. Second, assuming eth_requestAccounts will always succeed is wrong — users can deny access. Your app must handle denials by remaining functional in a read-only mode or prompting clearly for next steps. Third, attempting to use JsonRpcProvider to sign transactions is a typical error; JsonRpcProvider is read-only unless combined with a signer that holds a private key. Fourth, exposing or requesting private keys in the frontend is a serious security mistake — wallets handle keys for a reason. Finally, not listening for account or chain changes will leave your UI showing stale information. A concrete remediation: implement graceful fallbacks, clear signers on account removal, and reload or reinitialize on chain change. Adopt these patterns to maintain both security and a reliable user experience. In this chapter we focus on the practical plumbing that lets a browser-based DApp speak to Ethereum. You will learn why libraries like web3. js and ethers. js exist, how they wrap the node JSON‑RPC A P I, and what a provider and a signer do for your application. We'll show concrete provider types you will use in the browser or from services like Infura and Alchemy, and we'll walk through a typical wallet connection flow so your frontend can read the network and ask the user to sign transactions. This matters because a correct provider and a secure signer are the difference between read-only data calls and safely sending state-changing transactions. For example, using a BrowserProvider lets MetaMask hold private keys while your app requests a signed transaction. A common trap is treating a JsonRpcProvider as if it could sign; it cannot. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to initialize ethers. js providers, request account access, fetch the current block number, and respond to account or chain changes with safe patterns. Think about your own DApp: what operations will require a signer, and which can use a read-only provider?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to name and use the main libraries that connect a DApp to Ethereum, initialize providers, and request a signer for transactions. First, you'll distinguish the roles of web3. js and ethers. js and why ethers. js is often chosen for frontend work. Second, you'll configure BrowserProvider for injected wallets and JsonRpcProvider for read‑only access, which is important when your app must fetch data without holding private keys. Third, you'll retrieve basic blockchain data such as the current block number and network ID so your UI can display accurate state. Finally, you'll recognize common connection pitfalls like missing window. ethereum or assuming a provider can sign. Each objective is practical and directly maps to tasks you will run in your project, ensuring your DApp can both read data and securely request signed transactions from users. Consider which objective you need first based on whether your app only reads data or must send signed transactions.

These secondary objectives build practical resilience into your DApp. You will practice requesting account access and updating UI state when accounts or networks change. You will also learn to choose when to use specialized providers such as InfuraProvider or AlchemyProvider to simplify configuration. These providers make it easier to connect to a public node endpoint without running your own node, which is important when you need reliable read access. You will also learn to detect the absence of an injected provider and present a clear prompt for the user to install a wallet. As a concrete example, you will implement a connection flow that calls eth_requestAccounts, reads the network name and block number, and listens for accountsChanged and chainChanged events. Think about how your app should behave if the user denies access — your app must handle that gracefully.

At the heart of a DApp's communication layer are libraries that hide the raw JSON‑RPC details and present a higher‑level A P I. web3. js and ethers. js both serve this role, but the chapter emphasizes that ethers. js was designed for a cleaner, modular developer experience. Conceptually both libraries translate method calls into JSON‑RPC requests that a node understands. For example, a call to get the current block number becomes a JSON‑RPC call the library abstracts away. A concrete example is calling provider. getBlockNumber in ethers. js: the library performs the RPC, returns a number, and allows your UI to display the latest block. A common misconception is that libraries add new network capabilities; they only wrap the node A P I and provide utilities like ABI encoding, contract binding, and convenience helpers. Another common confusion is believing one library is more secure simply by name; security comes from correct usage, provider choice, and not exposing private keys. Closing thought: when choosing a library, prioritize the A P I ergonomics and the patterns that match your stack, especially if you use TypeScript and want stronger type guarantees.

Both libraries provide the same core capability: talk to Ethereum nodes. The chapter emphasizes their design differences. web3. js is older and very comprehensive; it bundles many modules and covers many interaction needs. ethers. js was built later with modularity, smaller bundles, and a focus on security and developer ergonomics, including TypeScript friendliness. A concrete example: when building a Vite React frontend, many developers prefer ethers. js because it is lighter to bundle and its BrowserProvider integrates nicely with an injected wallet. A common mistake is choosing a library solely on age or popularity; instead evaluate A P I ergonomics, size, and TypeScript support that match your stack. Closing question: which matters more for your project — a feature-heavy A P I or smaller client size and clearer TypeScript types? A BrowserProvider wraps an injected window. ethereum object offered by wallet extensions such as MetaMask and enables the wallet to manage keys and sign transactions.
